question: How can I use an hybridization of ontology and machine learning for text summarization ?

sections.title: System Architecture
sections.text: The OATS cognitive system integrates ontology and machine learning into two distinct modules for automatic text summarization [1]. The first module performs ontology-based topic identification to select relevant documents aligned with user interests [1][1]. The second module generates user-focused summaries by exploiting answers extracted from a machine learning-based question-answering model [1][1]. This hybrid approach allows the system to leverage structured knowledge for document retrieval and statistical models for content extraction [1][1].

sections.title: Ontology and Graph Construction
sections.text: The system utilizes a simplified COVID-19 Risk Factor ontology, which is a reduced version of a Clinical Quality Measure (CQM) ontology that excludes the "Change Concept" component [3] [4][1]. This ontology is motivated by prior work by Schwemmer et al. (2019), who manually extracted "gold standard" concept graphs from approximately 2,000 CQM descriptions to guide concept selection [1]. In the current implementation, the igraph package in the R programming language is used to create graph concepts from extracted triples [2]. A matching algorithm then determines the relevancy of each document to specific risk factors using these graph representations [1][1].

sections.title: Machine Learning Components
sections.text: Document relevancy scoring is performed using a word2vec model trained on ten years of data to assess the connection between documents and specific risk factors [5]. Because common words are filtered out during processing, there is no need for IDF normalization in the scoring process [1]. For the summarization phase, a sentence scoring method was developed to improve generation performance, particularly when extracted answers appear in multiple sentences [1]. This ML component complements the ontology-based retrieval by providing the specific content required for the final summary [1][1].

sections.title: Matching Algorithm and Performance
sections.text: The matching algorithm demonstrates varying performance across different risk factors. Hypertension achieved a precision of 0.93 and a recall of 0.84, while Diabetes reached a precision of 0.92 and a recall of 0.76 [1][1]. Obesity showed perfect precision at 1.0 but a lower recall of 0.71 [1]. Performance was slightly poorer for COPD, with a precision of 0.81 and a recall of 0.60 [1][1]. To address the low recall associated with acronyms, the system separates "COPD" into its four constituent words and measures the distance from each word to candidate terms, although this can lower precision due to commonplace terms like "chronic" [1].

sections.title: QA Model Limitations and Context
sections.text: The question-answering model requires a standardized set of questions to access information that may be presented in non-standardized ways across documents [1]. Extraction accuracy is sensitive to question wording, especially when information is presented slightly differently in various sources [1]. Additionally, inaccessibility to text sections containing optimal answers limits model performance [1]. Specifically, odds ratios are often presented in tables, which are not included in the text available to the QA model, affecting questions Q7 and Q8 [1]. Despite these limitations, extracted answers pertaining to methodology information (Q1 through Q6) achieved over 50% accuracy [1]. This work builds upon prior research, including Arumae & Liu (2019), who developed a supervised deep learning framework using human-annotated question-answer pairs, and Muresan et al. (2001), who combined linguistic and machine learning techniques for email summarization [1][6].

question: How can the integration of GIS spatial analysis techniques with economic modeling improve the accuracy and effectiveness of environmental policy ?

sections.title: Foundations of Spatial-Economic Integration
sections.text: The integration of spatial statistical analysis with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) offers a sophisticated framework for regional economic analysis [2]. Spatial statistics provides the theoretical basis for conducting exploratory analysis and making inferences on spatial data [3]. This approach allows researchers to move between different geographical scales, such as shifting from small units to larger regions, while capturing the impact of broader areas on specific components [2]. By connecting environmental and economic data through linked data structures, analysts can address the critical need to integrate environmental information with administrative, political, social, and economic datasets for development policy [1]. Numerous attempts have been made to reinforce the analysis of spatial-econ.

sections.title: Methodological Approaches and Prediction
sections.text: Environmental modeling activities can significantly benefit from GIS technology [4]. The integration of environmental models with GIS functionalities can be achieved through either loosely or tightly coupled approaches [4]. Spatial prediction methods are generally categorized into spatial classification for categorical responses and spatial regression for continuous responses [3]. To simplify these prediction methods, it is often assumed that spatial homogeneity exists, characterized by stationarity and isotropy. These statistical tools enhance the ability to model complex spatial relationships that traditional non-spatial models might overlook.

sections.title: System Dynamics and Policy Application
sections.text: System dynamics (SD) theory has long been used to model complex non-linear interrelationships [6]. However, the use of SD modeling to support the practical implementation of environmental sustainability policies has not been common [6]. A primary reason for this gap is that the challenge of incorporating spatial data into SD modeling has not yet been adequately addressed [6]. The potential for combining SD and GIS methods is exemplified in studies that integrate an economic model of climate change with a small structural model of the Greenland ice sheet (GIS) [6] [5]. This integration provides a methodology for incorporating large earth system changes into standard economic cost-benefit or damage-limiting analyses [5].

sections.text: Policy analysis in the environmental field has improved in various ways by internalizing spatial-environmental externalities, for example, through Pigouvian taxation schemes [7]. This combined approach allows for more accurate assessments of how local actions affect larger regional systems, thereby improving the precision of cost-benefit analyses and the design of targeted regulatory interventions.

question: Have specialized approaches been developed for providing LLM assistance when people author SQL queries?

sections.title: Necessity of Specialized SQL Approaches
sections.text: Treating SQL as a standard programming language for existing LLM autocompletion systems is insufficient due to three main challenges that warrant special treatment [1]. A primary difficulty is that coexisting with traditional autocomplete systems remains a significant hurdle for many AI-assisted code authoring solutions [1]. Furthermore, the focus of specialized work is on autocompleting SQL queries as authors type them out, rather than general generation [1]. This iterative nature is critical because the biggest time savings and productivity boosts come from helping developers bootstrap and iterate on complex SQL queries without navigating clunky syntax, semantics, or documentation [1].

sections.title: Latency and Efficiency Constraints
sections.text: Latency constraints are much tighter for an autocompletion tool compared to natural language querying [1]. This issue is pronounced in LLM-based text-to-SQL systems, where generating SQL queries is slower than traditional language modeling, posing a challenge for developing efficient, localized NL interfaces to databases (NLIDB) [2]. To address this, Consistency large language models (CLLMs) have been developed with an enhanced model architecture, providing a solution to reduce latency and speed up SQL query generation [2]. Additionally, LCM overcomes the limitations imposed by regular CM objective with respect to tokenization [1].

sections.title: Schema Linking and Retrieval Strategies
sections.text: Prompting LLMs with entire schemas alongside the user's question fails on large databases [4]. To mitigate this, SchemaGraphSQL offers efficient schema linking using pathfinding graph algorithms for text-to-sql on large-scale databases [5]. Another approach involves scaling Text2SQL via LLM-efficient schema filtering using Functional Dependency Graph Rerankers [4]. RAG-based text-to-SQL systems also integrate dynamic retrieval abilities with generative models to improve SQL query generation [2]. While LLMs excel at row-level inference because they can reason over context and semantics [3], these retrieval and filtering methods are necessary to manage the complexity of large schemas.

question: How can question generation be used to mitigate hallucination in LLMs?

sections.title: Retrieval-Based Mitigation via Question-to-Question Matching
sections.text: A primary strategy for eliminating hallucination involves bypassing the generative step entirely by leveraging question-to-question (Q2Q) retrieval. Traditional methods suffer from low semantic similarity because questions are interrogative while source passages are declarative, a structural disparity that hinders high-precision retrieval [1]. To resolve this, the Q2Q approach employs an instruction-tuned LLM to generate a comprehensive set of questions for each logical content unit within a knowledge base, rather than embedding the document content directly [1]. For knowledge graphs like Wikidata, the system generates all possible questions to make entity relations accessible to a question-answering system [1]. This method achieves high cosine similarity (>0.9) for relevant question pairs, enabling precise retrieval [1]. By directly retrieving original content instead of relying on generated answers, the response is hallucination-free [1]. While this avoids the risk of the LLM creating plausible but incorrect answers, addressing the initial retrieval challenge may still require strategies such as question reformulation, passage summarization, or hybrid approaches combining semantic search with keyword matching [1].

A promising direction for mitigating this is to fine-tune LLMs to better align with source constraints. sections.title: Self-Estimation and Hallucination Testing Frameworks
sections.text: Another avenue for reducing hallucination involves optimizing API dependency through self-estimation. A proposed LLM is able to self-estimate if it is able to answer directly or needs to request an external tool [6]. This supervised approach introduces a hallucination masking mechanism where labels are generated using a close-book question-answering task [6]. The model directly provides answers for 78.2% of the known queries and opts to search for 77.2% of the unknown ones [6]. Consequently, the external API is utilized only 62% of the time, balancing accuracy with resource efficiency [6]. Furthermore, to evaluate the effectiveness of these models, researchers have presented a novel framework for generating invalid questions to test the frequency of hallucinations output by new LLMs [5]. This involves collecting an augmented version of the DBpedia dataset replaced with invalid questions to measure overfitting and hallucination rates.

sections.title: Representation of Demonstrations in DSLs
sections.text: Programming by Demonstration (PbD) is an approach for faster software development in domains where the user works interactively with a computer or some machinery [5]. This method has been adopted by many tools to reduce the expertise required, as users only have to interact with the target applications rather than write code [4]. To support programming for tasks in diverse domains, systems leverage the graphical user interfaces (GUIs) of existing third-party mobile apps as a medium, where procedural actions are represented as sequences of GUI operations [3]. Declarative concepts can be represented through references to GUI contents [3]. The system focuses on intuitive symbolic representations like a domain specific language (DSL) or a natural language interface [2].
